lede: Three brackets multiplied together is two brackets multiplied together, twice. Expand any pair, collect, then multiply the quadratic you are left with by the bracket still waiting. Six products come out of that second step, and counting them is how you know none has gone missing.
can: Expand a pair of brackets and collect the result into a quadratic.
Multiply a three-term quadratic by a linear bracket, all six products.
Write the cubic down in descending powers, and check both ends.

md: Three brackets in a row is the one piece of pure algebra CCEA prints almost every year, early in the paper and usually for three marks. It is also what the rest of Unit 1 is built on: a cubic you expanded yourself is what you differentiate later, and it is where the volume in a box problem comes from. The marks that go are lost to a dropped term or a lost sign.

caption: Six products come out of the second grid. Counting them is the fastest check that none has been dropped.

prompt: One tap to start. When $(x+1)(x+2)$ is multiplied out, what is the constant term?
explain: The constant can only come from $1 \times 2$. That one idea — the constant term is the product of the constants — is about to do a lot of work.

md:
You already know how to multiply two brackets. Three is the same job done twice, because a product can be grouped any way you like: $abc$ means $(ab)c$ and $a(bc)$ equally.
So **pick any two brackets, expand and collect**. That leaves a quadratic times a linear bracket. Then **multiply every term of the quadratic by every term of the bracket** — three terms times two terms is six products — and collect like terms into descending powers.
Choosing the easy pair first is allowed and often saves a line. If one bracket is $(3-x)$, leave it exactly as printed rather than reversing it.

prompt: A quadratic with three terms multiplies a bracket with two terms. How many products before you collect?
explain: Three times two. If you have fewer than six products written down, a term has been missed, and that is the single commonest way this question loses a mark.

md:
Before you expand anything, you can write down both ends of the answer.
The $x^{3}$ term can only come from the three $x$ terms multiplied together. The constant can only come from the three numbers multiplied together. Nothing else can reach either end.
So for $(x+2)(x-5)(3x-1)$ the cubic term is $3x^{3}$ and the constant is $10$ — two negatives multiplied. If your expansion disagrees with either, stop and find the missing product before you go on.

prompt: What is the constant term in the expansion of $(x-2)(x+4)(x-3)$?
explain: $(-2) \times 4 \times (-3)$. Two negative brackets leave the constant positive; one would leave it negative.

title: Why both ends can be written first
md: An $x^{3}$ can only be made by multiplying the three $x$ terms together, because every other product uses at least one constant and so comes out at a lower power. The constant is the mirror image: it is the one product that uses no $x$ at all.

title: Expanding Three Brackets
why: Five minutes of the two-at-a-time routine written out at the speed of a hand. Watch it once, then answer the gate below without scrolling back.

explain: The second option uses only the $x$ from the last bracket. The third keeps the first terms and the last terms and throws the middle away. Both have the right $x^{3}$ term, which is why they look plausible.

title: Summer 2022, FM1 Q9(a)
md: A cubic and a quadratic were expanded correctly by most candidates, and then the final mark went because the quadratic was not subtracted in full. Examiners asked for brackets round the subtracted expression. A second group reached the right answer and then divided it by 2, turning a correct expansion into an expression that was no longer equal to it.

prompt: You have expanded a cubic and now have to subtract a quadratic from it. What do you write first?
options: The quadratic inside brackets, with the minus sign in front of the bracket
The quadratic with its first term's sign changed
The two expressions side by side and collect straight away
answer: The quadratic inside brackets, with the minus sign in front of the bracket
explain: Then remove the bracket on the next line, changing every sign inside it. The bracket is what makes the sign change apply to all of it, and it is the line the examiners asked for.

md:
Expand any pair of brackets and collect.
Multiply that quadratic by the bracket left over, all six products.
Collect into descending powers, and check both ends.

The wording is almost always **Expand and simplify the expression**, for three marks: one for a correct pair expanded, one for multiplying that quadratic by the remaining bracket, one for the collected answer in descending powers. Write the first pair out even if you can see nothing else. Stuck: expand a different pair — the answer is the same whichever you start with, and the second pair is often kinder.
